name: PICA Portland
overview: Portland Institute for Contemporary Art, a contemporary art organisation at 15 NE Hancock Street, Portland, Oregon.
Founded in 1995 by Kristy Edmunds while she directed the Portland Art Museum's Art on the Edge program. PICA first worked from vacant or rented spaces around Portland (Wikipedia).
Its annual Time-Based Art Festival (TBA) began in September 2003 and uses venues across the city. TBA:26 runs 9 to 13 September 2026.
funding_verdict: PICA Portland: mainly private giving: foundations, individuals and companies, with state arts money

name: Mingei International Museum
overview: Mingei International Museum, 1439 El Prado, Balboa Park, San Diego (museum website).
The About page says Mingei was founded in 1978 (museum website).
What is there: the page read gives no object count; it describes a partial gallery closure with discounted admission while new exhibitions are installed (museum website).
funding_verdict: Mingei International Museum: mainly private contributions, funders not named in the pages read

name: The Timken Museum of Art
overview: Timken Museum of Art, 1500 El Prado, Balboa Park, San Diego; administrative office at 2550 Fifth Avenue, Suite 500 (museum website).

It opened in 1965. Two families made it possible: the Timken family of Canton, Ohio, and sisters Anne and Amy Putnam; the Timken Foundation paid for a large part of the new picture gallery (museum website, History page).

What is there: the Putnam Collection of European old masters, American art and Russian icons. In 1950 the Putnam sisters, advised by attorney Walter Ames, set up a foundation to acquire 'paintings of high quality'; its works were loaned to museums across the country until the Timken opened (museum website, History page).
funding_verdict: The Timken Museum of Art: founded on Timken and Putnam family money; current funding not stated in the pages read

name: San José Museum of Art
aliases: San Jose Museum of Art Association
overview: San José Museum of Art, 110 South Market Street, San Jose (address from OpenStreetMap).
The pages read did not give its founding history, collection or archive.
funding_verdict: San José Museum of Art: mainly contributions, funders not named in the pages read

name: SITE Santa Fe
overview: Contemporary art institution at 1606 Paseo de Peralta in Santa Fe's Railyard district (SITE Santa Fe; Metropolis, 2017).

Established on 1 February 1995 to host a contemporary art biennial. The local gallery owner Laura Carpenter conceived the idea in 1992 and raised more than $1 million in donations (Wikipedia). The first biennial opened on 14 July 1995, curated by Bruce W. Ferguson with Vince Varga (Wikipedia).
Its flagship exhibition is the SITE SANTA FE International Biennial, listed on its site as the International (SITE Santa Fe).
funding_verdict: SITE Santa Fe: mainly contributions: donors, a Business Council of local firms and benefit sponsors

name: Schweikher House
overview: House museum at 645 Meacham Road in Schaumburg, Illinois, reached by a long gravel driveway, and the only listing on the National Register of Historic Places in Schaumburg (the house's site).

The architect Paul Schweikher built it as his home and studio in 1937 to 1938 and called it "South Willow". English Wikipedia says he sold it to the physicist Alexander Langsdorf and the artist Martyl Langsdorf in 1953, while the house's site says they rented from 1953 and bought in 1956. Martyl designed the Doomsday Clock cover and died in Schaumburg in 2013.
Named for its architect, Paul Schweikher. English Wikipedia says it is also called the Schweikher-Langsdorf Home and Studio.
funding_verdict: Schweikher House: mainly public ownership and small donations: the Village of Schaumburg owns it, a village-appointed trust runs it

name: Henry Art Gallery
overview: Museum of contemporary art on the west edge of the University of Washington campus, along 15th Avenue N.E. in the University District (Wikipedia).
Founded by Horace C. Henry, who funded the museum and donated 178 artworks. It opened to the public on 10 February 1927 and was the first public art museum in Washington state (Wikipedia).
Named for Horace C. Henry. From 1917 he had run a wing of his Capitol Hill home as a free museum (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Henry Art Gallery: mixed public and private: University of Washington administration, city, county and state arts agencies, federal grants, foundations and sponsors

press_items.title: Jen Graves, "When Did the Henry Art Gallery Fall Asleep?" (4 October 2016)
Matthew Offenbacher, "Seattle Museums Are Artwashing Their Way Back to Normal" (12 October 2021)

name: Pulitzer Arts Foundation
overview: Art museum at 3716 Washington Boulevard, St. Louis, in the Grand Center Arts District, presenting historical and contemporary art from around the world (pulitzerarts.org).
Founded in 2001 by Emily Rauh Pulitzer, with her husband Joseph Pulitzer Jr., who died in 1993 before construction began in 1996 (Wikipedia; Washington University commencement archive).
Richard Serra's courtyard sculpture "Joe" is named for the late Joseph Pulitzer Jr. (pulitzerarts.org).
funding_verdict: Pulitzer Arts Foundation: privately run: the founding family's foundation, free to visit; sources of revenue not published

name: Everson Museum of Art
aliases: Everson Museum of Art of Syracuse and Onondaga County
overview: An art museum at 401 Harrison Street, Syracuse, New York, in a building by I.M. Pei that opened in 1968 and that the museum calls his first museum design (museum website).
Its roots are the Syracuse Museum of Fine Arts, founded in 1897 by George Fisk Comfort; Helen Everson's 1941 bequest led to the Everson Museum of Art, chartered in 1949 (museum website, About).

What is there: approximately 11,000 works focused on American modern and contemporary art, including paintings, ceramics, sculpture, video, photographs, works on paper and decorative arts; ceramics and video art are core collections, and the ceramics holding began in 1916 with 32 porcelains by Adelaide Alsop Robineau, with the Ceramic National exhibitions established in 1932 (museum website, Our Collection).
funding_verdict: Everson Museum of Art: private donations and investment income, with a campaign and named funds

name: Marcel Breuer House at Pocantico
overview: House on the grounds of the Pocantico Center, run by the Rockefeller Brothers Fund, in Pocantico Hills near Tarrytown, New York (Glass House).

Marcel Breuer's house was commissioned in 1948 for an exhibition in the garden of the Museum of Modern Art. When the show closed it was due to be demolished. John D. Rockefeller Jr. bought it, had it cut into four sections and trucked it to Pocantico Hills, where it was reassembled as a guest house. Rockefeller family members used it as a guest house from 1950 to 2007 (Glass House).
Named for its architect. The Glass House page gives no earlier name and no date for the move.
funding_verdict: Marcel Breuer House: foundation-funded: the Rockefeller Brothers Fund, with the National Trust as owner

name: Tucson Museum of Art
aliases: Tucson Museum of Art and Historic Block
overview: Tucson Museum of Art, 140 North Main Avenue, Tucson (museum website).

What is there: collection areas are Art of the American West, Asian Art, Contemporary Art, Decorative Arts, European Art, Indigenous Arts, Latin American Art and Modern Art; the page gives no object count (museum website).
The pages read did not give a founding year or describe an archive.
funding_verdict: Tucson Museum of Art: contributions and earned income, funders not named in the pages read

name: Iñupiat Heritage Center
overview: Museum and cultural centre at 5421 N Star St, Utqiaġvik, on Alaska's North Slope (National Park Service; North Slope Borough).
Dedicated in February 1999 (National Park Service).

An affiliated area of New Bedford Whaling National Historical Park in Massachusetts: one of several partners that tell the story of commercial whaling and of the Alaska Natives who crewed, fed, clothed and sheltered the Yankee whalers (National Park Service).
funding_verdict: Iñupiat Heritage Center: public: the North Slope Borough, funded mainly by taxes on oil and gas infrastructure
wider_context: Alaska Public Media reported in March 2019 that ConocoPhillips was pushing three new oil projects in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska, Willow and Greater Moose's Tooth 1 and 2, and that projected royalty and property tax revenue from the reserve could reach $700 million a year for the borough and its villages.
Connection: the borough budget that pays for the centre grows with that oil development.

name: Dumbarton Oaks
aliases: Dumbarton Oaks Research Library and Collection
overview: Dumbarton Oaks is an estate near Washington given to Harvard University by Robert Woods Bliss in 1940 (The Harvard Crimson, 1962).
It hosted preliminary United Nations conferences and houses Harvard's programmes in pre-Columbian art and Byzantine studies (The Harvard Crimson, 1962).
What is there and Archive: the pages read gave no object or archive counts.
funding_verdict: Dumbarton Oaks: privately endowed through the Bliss gift to Harvard; current funders not stated in the pages read

name: The Kreeger Museum
overview: The Kreeger Museum is at 2401 Foxhall Road NW, Washington DC, in a travertine-clad building designed in 1963 by Philip Johnson and Richard Foster, on five acres with sculpture gardens and terraces (museum website, history page).

David and Carmen Kreeger began assembling a collection of modern art in 1959 and over the next fifteen years put together most of the museum's holdings; the museum bears their name (museum website, history page).

What is there: works from the 1850s to the present, including nine Claude Monet paintings, Renoir, Sisley, Pissarro, Picasso across his career, Munch, Beckmann, Dubuffet, Kandinsky, Miro, Calder, Clyfford Still, Frank Stella and James Rosenquist, plus Washington artists William Christenberry, Gene Davis, Sam Gilliam and others. The sculpture terrace has Arp, Maillol, Lipchitz, Henry Moore and Noguchi, and the collection also holds African and Asian art (museum website, collection page).
funding_verdict: The Kreeger Museum: founding family collection and house; current funders not named on the pages read

name: IZOLYATSIA
overview: Non-profit cultural platform, now based in Kyiv on the site of the Kyiv Shipbuilding and Ship Repair Plant on Naberezhno-Luhova Street (Wikipedia). It describes itself as a "non-profit, non-governmental platform for cultural initiatives" (IZOLYATSIA).

Founded in 2010 in a former insulation works in Donetsk (IZOLYATSIA). Wikipedia names Lyubov Mikhailova, daughter of the last Soviet director of an insulation materials plant on that territory, as founder.

On 9 June 2014 armed members of the Donetsk People's Republic took over the foundation's premises, and it relocated to Kyiv. Only part of the exhibits left Donetsk. The library, equipment, shop and works that could not be moved were destroyed or looted (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: IZOLYATSIA: grant-funded with private backing: EU programmes, international grants and its owner Liubov Mykhaylova (Kyiv Post, 2016)

name: PinchukArtCentre
overview: Private contemporary art centre in a historic architectural complex in Kyiv's Besarabka area, with interiors by the French architect Philippe Chiambaretta (centre website).
Founded by the businessman Victor Pinchuk in September 2006 (centre website); it opened on 16 September 2006 (Wikipedia).
It occupies six floors: exhibition space on four, more than 3,000 square metres in all, plus a library, an education room and a video lounge (centre website).
funding_verdict: PinchukArtCentre: self-funded: founder Victor Pinchuk and his foundation
wider_context: In 2004 Pinchuk and Rinat Akhmetov bought the Kryvorizhstal steel plant for about $800 million; Pinchuk's father-in-law, President Leonid Kuchma, authorised the sale, which competitors said was far below market rate (Wikipedia).

The plant was returned to the state in June 2005 after the government challenged the privatisation, which President Viktor Yushchenko called a theft; on 24 October 2005 Mittal Steel bought it at a televised auction for more than $4.8 billion (AP, via NBC News).

A 2007 cable by US ambassador William B. Taylor said the Nikopol Ferroalloy Plant tenders of 2003 and 2004 were "rigged in favor of" Pinchuk, "like the subsequent sale of the Kryvorizhstal steel plant" (Kyiv Post).

Guides who formed a union in October 2019 protested near the centre on 25 December 2019; their fixed-term contracts were not renewed and on 9 February 2020 the centre abolished the post (Wikipedia). The Art Newspaper counted 28 guides dismissed, the Kyiv Post about 20. Artists Valentina Petrova and Pavlo Grazhdanskij withdrew from the 2020 PinchukArtCentre Prize in solidarity (The Art Newspaper).

The Trump Foundation's 2015 tax return showed $150,000 from Pinchuk's London-based charity; his press service said in November 2016 that it paid for Donald Trump's video call to the Yalta European Strategy conference, which the Victor Pinchuk Foundation organises (UNIAN, citing Fast Company and Ukrayinska Pravda).

Unverified: Ihor Kolomoisky told a parliamentary hearing in March 2015 that Pinchuk took $5 million a month for the right to manage Ukrnafta; the National Anti-Corruption Bureau opened criminal proceedings on 18 March 2015 (Wikipedia).
These concern the founder's business and politics, and the centre's own staff before November 2021.

press_items.title: Dorian Batycka, "PinchukArtCenter employees claim to have been sacked after attempting to form trade union" (2020)
Toma Istomina, "Pinchuk Art Center mediators lose jobs after forming union" (2020)
artur.sumarokov, "The Pinchuk Art Centre: Two Decades of Cynical Art-Washing for Ukraine's Most Polished Oligarch" (2026)

name: Museo Nacional de Artes Visuales
overview: National art museum at Tomás Giribaldi 2283, corner of Julio Herrera y Reissig, in Parque Rodó, Montevideo.
It later became the Museo Nacional de Artes Visuales. Its first year was in the left wing of the Teatro Solís.
Its original collection was 234 pieces, mostly foreign. Its collection traces back to the Museo y Biblioteca Nacional, founded on 18 July 1838 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Museo Nacional de Artes Visuales: mainly public: the Uruguayan state, through the Ministry of Education and Culture

name: Nha San Collective
overview: Non-profit, artist-run group for experimental and contemporary art in Hanoi.
Formed in 2013 by younger artists from Nhà Sàn Studio. Wikipedia credits Nguyen Phuong Linh and Tuan Mami as co-founders.

Takes its name from Nhà Sàn Studio, founded in 1998 by Nguyễn Mạnh Đức and Trần Lương in Nguyễn's family home, a stilt house. The collective's site says the house was taken in 2020 and that the artists hope to rebuild a space in the Ngọc Thụy area by the Red River.
funding_verdict: Nha San Collective: volunteer-run: private donations and cultural institutions in Vietnam and abroad (stated by the collective)
wider_context: Art Asia Pacific (1 November 2018, unsigned, "Hanoi") says Nha San Studio was shut in 2011 following state pressure tied to a nude performance. The Yale Globalist (Josh Feng, "Bound to Shackles," 2014) puts a closure in 2010 after a displayed work depicted nudity. The sources differ on the year.

Prachatai (Julia Behrens, "Free of art or freedom of art: Nha San collective's struggle for space in Vietnam," 2015) says the group has been shut down many times, avoids registering as a formal institution, and still needs permission for public activities.

Residency Unlimited, describing a 13 June 2019 talk on Vietnam's contemporary art scene, says the field "still receives little support from the government" and increasingly relies on private and corporate money.
It is the successor to the studio that was closed, and it is the group these pieces describe.

name: Sàn Art
aliases: san art ho chi minh city
overview: Independent, artist-initiated, non-profit contemporary art organisation in Ho Chi Minh City. The name "sàn" means "platform" (benefit auction announcement, e-flux, December 2014).

Founded in October 2007 (e-flux). The first exhibition opened on 3 October 2007 (Zoe Butt, SFMOMA Open Space, 27 September 2012). The four founders are Dinh Q. Lê, Tuan Andrew Nguyen, Phu Nam Thuc Ha (Phunam) and Tiffany Chung (Courtney Malick, SFAQ, 10 October 2014).
It began as a reading room and international lecture programme, and later added curated exhibitions, an artist residency, workshops and talks (e-flux).
funding_verdict: Sàn Art (Ho Chi Minh City): donor and benefit-auction funded: international organisations and individuals; Sàn Art states that Vietnam gives it no financial support

name: Nhaka Gallery (formerly Gallery Delta)
overview: Nhaka Gallery & Creative Space, at 110 Livingstone Road, Greenwood Park, Harare. It is run by the Women's Gallery Arts and Research Trust and, in the article's words, aims to build "a creative, safe, dynamic space for nurturing Zimbabwe's next generation of artists" (Greedy South, Tafadzwa Madzika, 11 March 2023).
The same article says the address was Gallery Delta until 2022 and that Delta's founders "helped young artists learn their craft, get international exposure, and launch their careers".

Gallery Delta was founded in 1975 by Derek Huggins, a former detective inspector with Rhodesia's British South Africa Police, and his wife, the artist Helen Lieros. It began in Strachan's building on Manica Road and moved in 1991 to 110 Livingstone Avenue, a house dating to 1894 offered by Colette Wiles, daughter of the painter Robert Paul (Wits University, Tinashe Mushakavanhu, 26 July 2021).
funding_verdict: Nhaka Gallery: trust-run, with embassy and UN Women support for one 2023 show
